newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-ITALIANS FACE UP TO CHANGING TIMES.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ITALIANS FACE UP TO CHANGING TIMES.

text.p: The state of Italian soccer has long been a national obsession but two deals in the space of one day last week have prompted renewed soul-searching and highlighted the changing face of serie A.

Those convinced that Italy still has the world's strongest and richest league were given reassurance on Friday when an agent for Ronaldo announced that the Brazilian striker had signed a five-year deal with Inter Milan.
Ronaldo's lawyer also said that the club had handed over $27.5 million merely to release the 20-year-old from his contract with Spanish club Barcelona.
The eventual sums to be paid out will make Ronaldo far and away the world's most expensive soccer star.
Ironically, those who worry that Italian soccer is being overtaken by new wealth flooding the English, German and Spanish leagues also received cause for concern.
Vicenza, a small but profitable provincial club, were sold at auction to British investment firm Stellican because of bankruptcy proceedings involving their owners.
The price was just $13.5 million and it made Vicenza, in next season's European Cup Winners' Cup, the first foreign-owned Italian club in a supposedly soccer-crazy country.

Some saw it all as a positive development, proof of the investment potential of Italian soccer beyond the local market and the changing nature of Italian clubs away from family fiefdoms towards big business and bourse listings.
Ronaldo's arrival is a business venture, just as Vicenza's take-over has a profit motive.
"The first reason to be satisfied is in the observation that Italian soccer has a notable appeal in England," said league president Franco Carraro.
"There are English businessmen ready and willing to invest in Italy and Italian soccer. That is a good thing."
"I think it's an interesting development, that in some ways reflects the fact that soccer is becoming increasingly international," said former Vicenza great Paolo Rossi.

"The main thing is that intentions are good...for the rest I would not worry too much that the new owners are not from Vicenza. The days of the do-it-all president, who maybe lives in the centre of town, are over.
"Soccer is now a global business, with mega-firms committed to publicising brands and carrying out medium-to-long term programmes," the 1982 World Cup hero said.

English immigrants brought soccer to Italy in the 19th century, creating the Genoa Cricket and Athletic club in 1893, and most newspapers commented on the irony of the founders returning a century later as buyers.
But others detected hints of malaise.
As Tuttosport newspaper pointed out, Vicenza cost the equivalent of having Ronaldo for just one year and yet nobody local could be found to purchase the club.
"The wealthiest part of Italy, the north-east, could not manage to buy a very good club of its own, a club heading into Europe after winning the Italian Cup," said Tuttosport.
The focus on Ronaldo and the apparent disinterest in a well-run provincial club also led to fears that local talent was being ignored for foreign glamour.
A decision on Thursday to allow Italian clubs to have five non-European Union players on their books, the most that any European league allows, worried unions particularly.

"It constitutes a very serious threat, with predictable consequences even in the short term for the technical identity of our soccer, for our national teams and youth programmes," said players' union leader Sergio Campana.
Some clubs, who can already field teams with few Italians, wanted the restrictions to be abandoned completely.
"Europeanism, freedom of movement, long live competition, soccer and economics without frontiers. We have to be coherent," wrote the editor of the Gazzetta dello Sport.

"We are getting used to situations that, only a short while ago, belonged to fantasy football: Like the serie A side without a national identity, with eight or 10 foreigners," editor Candido Cannavo added in a front page column.
But he said the unknown caused concern.
All Italian papers asked who was behind Stellican, with the firm's managing director Stephen Julius quoted as saying that his backers included "a major European soccer club."
The sale came after a season marked by Italians moving abroad to clubs they would never previously have considered.
As late as 1995, there were no Italian internationals playing abroad and coach Giovanni Trapattoni had come home after a frustrating time at Bayern Munich.
Before the Bosman ruling, the age of television megadeals and big bourse listings in Britain, it would have been unthinkable for a serie A club to be foreign owned.
Last year, Italian internationals Gianfranco Zola, Fabrizio Ravanelli and Roberto Di Matteo all went to England, joined by more and more compatriots as the season unfolded.
Glasgow Rangers, a club that once never signed Catholic players, now has three Italians on its books.
Italian clubs' bourse listings are on the way and top coaches have been broadening their horizons.
At the start of last season, four Italians with experience of winning the title were active in league soccer.
All four won titles again -- But only Marcello Lippi with Juventus was in Italy. The other three were abroad.
Fabio Capello won in Spain with Real Madrid, Trapattoni back at Bayern in Germany and former Napoli coach Albertino Bigon at Sion in Switzerland with a league and cup double.
Capello is returning to AC Milan but another highly-successful coach has left with Nevio Scala of Perugia taking over at European Cup holders Borussia Dortmund.
"Football is the new frontier for our exports," said the daily Il Giornale newspaper on Sunday.
"First it was the ice-cream makers and the pizza chefs, then the soccer players. Now it's the coaches' turn."
